questions.question: Which class of microorganisms is acellular and needs a host cell to multiply?
questions.explanation: Viruses are acellular (not composed of cells) and are obligate intracellular parasites, meaning they must enter a host cell to replicate. They cannot multiply on their own.

questions.question: Who proposed in 1546 that disease spreads by \seeds\ passed by contact, objects or air?
questions.explanation: Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546 suggested that epidemic diseases are caused by transferable \seeds\ (seminaria) that can spread by direct contact, contaminated objects (fomites), or through the air.

questions.question: Leeuwenhoek's \animalcules\ were:
options: Fragments of dead plant tissue seen in thin slices of cork
Tiny living things seen in pond water and plaque
Chemical crystals formed when pond water was evaporated
Mould spores carried on the surface of fresh meat
questions.explanation: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek observed tiny living organisms (\animalcules\) in pond water and dental plaque using his single-lens microscopes. These were among the first observations of bacteria and protists.

questions.question: Who introduced the word \cell\ in *Micrographia* (1665)?
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke coined the term \cell\ in his book *Micrographia* (1665) after observing the tiny compartments in thin slices of cork under a microscope.

questions.question: What did Redi's 1668 meat-jar experiment conclude?
options: Microbes enter jars only through the gauze covering
Maggots arise from rotting meat itself when it is warm
A vital force turns decaying meat into living larvae
questions.explanation: Francesco Redi showed that maggots appeared on meat only when flies could lay eggs on it. Sealed jars or jars covered with gauze remained maggot-free, supporting biogenesis (life from pre-existing life) and refuting spontaneous generation.

questions.question: Spallanzani's 1768 experiments differed from Needham's by:
options: Using swan-neck flasks open to the air
Adding carbolic acid to the broth before sealing
Infecting chickens with the cultured broth
questions.explanation: Lazzaro Spallanzani boiled his infusions for a longer time and sealed the flasks, whereas John Needham boiled briefly and left flasks open or loosely sealed. Spallanzani's stricter technique resulted in sterile flasks, supporting biogenesis.

questions.question: In Pasteur's experiment, microbes appeared in the broth when:
options: The flask was cooled below room temperature overnight
Fresh air was blown gently across the open end
The broth was boiled a second time after several months
The neck was broken or the flask tilted
questions.explanation: Microbial growth occurred only when the broth came into contact with the trapped dust/microbes, which happened when the neck was broken or the flask was tilted to allow the broth to touch the contaminated curve.

questions.question: Biogenesis is the principle that:
options: Life arises only from pre-existing life
Life arises spontaneously from decaying non-living matter
Life arises from a vital force acting on sterile broth
Life arises when air contacts heated organic infusions
questions.explanation: Biogenesis states that living organisms arise from other living organisms, not from non-living matter. This principle was established through the experiments of Redi, Spallanzani, and Pasteur.

questions.question: A pure culture is:
options: A mixed population of several bacterial species grown together on agar
Cells descended from one cell, free of other species
Any broth culture that has been heated to destroy all spores present
A sample taken directly from a patient without any further isolation steps
questions.explanation: A pure culture contains only one species of microorganism, all descended from a single cell. It is essential for studying the properties of a specific microbe.

questions.question: Tyndallisation refers to:
options: A single brief heating that preserves the flavour of foods and drinks
Filtration of liquids through porous porcelain to remove all bacteria
Repeated heating to kill spores in infusions
Exposure of surfaces to carbolic acid spray in operating theatres
questions.explanation: Tyndallisation (fractional sterilisation) involves heating an infusion at 100°C on three successive days. The first heating kills vegetative cells; spores that germinate overnight are killed on subsequent heatings.

questions.question: Pasteurisation is best defined as:
options: Prolonged boiling under pressure to destroy all spores and viruses
Repeated heating on three consecutive days to kill heat-resistant spores
Chemical treatment of wounds to kill microbes on living tissue
Mild controlled heating that kills spoilage organisms
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation is a mild heat treatment (e.g., 63°C for 30 min or 72°C for 15 s) that kills most spoilage organisms and some pathogens, but not all spores. It is used for milk and other foods.

questions.question: Semmelweis reduced deaths from childbed fever from about 18% to about 2% by:
options: Spraying carbolic acid in the delivery theatre
Removing the handle of a contaminated water pump
questions.explanation: Ignaz Semmelweis observed that doctors who performed autopsies and then attended deliveries carried \cadaveric particles\ to mothers. He instituted handwashing with chlorinated lime, which drastically reduced mortality from puerperal fever.

questions.question: Snow's 1854 cholera map is regarded as the foundation of:
questions.explanation: Snow's systematic mapping and analysis of cholera cases is considered a founding event in epidemiology—the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations.

questions.question: Lister introduced antiseptic surgery in 1867 using:
questions.explanation: Joseph Lister used carbolic acid (phenol) as an antiseptic to kill microbes in the operating theatre, greatly reducing surgical infections.

questions.question: Asepsis refers to:
options: Killing microbes on the surface of living tissue with chemicals
Weakening a pathogen so that it stimulates immunity
Treating disease with chemicals that inhibit the pathogen
questions.explanation: Asepsis means preventing microorganisms from entering a sterile environment or wound. It contrasts with antisepsis, which uses chemicals to kill microbes on living tissue.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Koch's postulates?
options: The microbe is present in every case of the disease and absent from healthy hosts
The microbe is isolated and grown in pure culture
The pure culture causes the same disease in a healthy host
The microbe must first be attenuated
questions.explanation: Koch's postulates do not include attenuation. They state that the microbe must be present in all cases, be isolated in pure culture, cause the disease when inoculated into a healthy host, and be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host.

questions.question: Which organism cannot be grown in pure culture, limiting the use of Koch's postulates?
questions.explanation: *Treponema pallidum* (the cause of syphilis) cannot be grown in pure culture in the laboratory, so Koch's postulates cannot be fully applied to it.

questions.question: Falkow's molecular Koch's postulates (1988) link disease to:
options: A vaccine and protective immunity in all hosts
An antibiotic and the organism that produced it in culture
A symptom and the season in which it most commonly occurs
questions.explanation: Falkow's molecular Koch's postulates extend Koch's postulates to the molecular level, linking a specific gene or virulence factor to the disease phenotype.

questions.question: The use of agar as a solid medium enabled:
options: Visualisation of viruses under the light microscope
Production of the first synthetic chemotherapeutic agent
Mapping of cholera cases in an urban district
Isolation of pure cultures on solid media
questions.explanation: Agar provides a solid surface for bacteria to grow as discrete colonies. This allows isolation of pure cultures from mixed samples, a critical advance in microbiology.

questions.question: The Gram stain (1884) is used to:
options: Distinguish bacteria into groups by staining
Kill bacteria on living tissue before surgery
Weaken pathogens for use in vaccines
Measure the genome size of bacteria through sequencing
questions.explanation: The Gram stain differentiates bacteria based on cell wall structure. Gram-positive bacteria stain purple; gram-negative bacteria stain pink.

questions.question: The word \vaccine\ comes from *vacca*, Latin for:
questions.explanation: Edward Jenner used material from cowpox lesions to protect against smallpox. The term vaccine comes from *vacca* (cow) and *vaccinia* (cowpox).

questions.question: Pasteur's vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies used:
questions.explanation: Louis Pasteur developed vaccines using attenuated (weakened) pathogens—for chicken cholera, anthrax, and rabies.

questions.question: Behring and Kitasato's serum therapy (1890) relied on:
options: Chemicals that kill pathogens with little harm to the host
Weakened live bacteria injected into healthy people
Mould extracts that inhibit bacterial growth
questions.explanation: Behring and Kitasato demonstrated that serum from animals immunized against diphtheria or tetanus contained antibodies (antitoxins) that neutralized the toxins. This led to serum therapy.

questions.question: Salvarsan, Ehrlich's \magic bullet\, was significant as the first:
questions.explanation: Paul Ehrlich developed Salvarsan (arsphenamine) as a synthetic chemical that could treat syphilis. It was the first synthetic chemotherapeutic agent.

questions.question: What did Fleming observe in 1928?
options: Staphylococcus colonies growing faster near a contaminating *Penicillium* mould
Complete death of *Penicillium* colonies surrounding a dense lawn of bacteria
Spontaneous appearance of mould in a sterile sealed flask of broth
questions.explanation: Alexander Fleming observed a zone of inhibition of bacterial growth around a contaminating *Penicillium* mould on a *Staphylococcus* plate. This led to the discovery of penicillin.

questions.question: Who purified penicillin and carried out its clinical trials?
questions.explanation: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain purified penicillin and conducted the first clinical trials, enabling its mass production.

questions.question: The term \antibiotic\ was coined by:
questions.explanation: Selman Waksman coined the term \antibiotic\ to describe chemical substances produced by microorganisms that inhibit or kill other microorganisms.

questions.question: Phagocytosis, described by Metchnikoff, is:
options: Engulfment of microbes by white blood cells
Neutralisation of toxins by specific circulating antibodies
Transfer of resistance genes between neighbouring bacterial cells
Destruction of microbes on skin by chemical disinfectants
questions.explanation: Élie Metchnikoff discovered phagocytosis, the process by which white blood cells (phagocytes) engulf and destroy microbes.

questions.question: Ivanovsky and Beijerinck are credited with the discovery of:
questions.explanation: Dmitri Ivanovsky and Martinus Beijerinck discovered viruses through their work on tobacco mosaic disease.

questions.question: Woese proposed the three domains of life (1977) based on:
questions.explanation: Carl Woese used rRNA sequence comparisons to propose the three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

questions.question: Which disease was eradicated worldwide in 1980?
questions.explanation: Smallpox was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980, following a global vaccination campaign.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as an emerging infection and an open challenge in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Lassa fever is an emerging viral hemorrhagic fever endemic in Nigeria and other West African countries. It poses a significant public health challenge.
